lessons.title: Detection-as-Code, Versioning, and Change Control
lessons.description: Production detection engineering benefits from source control, peer review, test fixtures, deployment automation, ownership, and rollback. This lesson teaches a practical lifecycle for maintaining rules as code artifacts.
learningObjectives: Explain why detection rules benefit from version control.
Structure a detection change for peer review and regression testing.
Track rule ownership, status, dependencies, and rollback information.
Identify changes that require revalidation, such as parser or schema changes.

notes.text: Minimal detection repository layout

detections/
  identity/
    password_spray.yml
  endpoint/
    suspicious_office_child.yml
  network/
    rare_outbound_destination.yml
tests/
  identity/
    password_spray_positive.jsonl
    password_spray_negative.jsonl
metadata/
  ownership.yml

items: Version the rule and its tests together.
Review logic, data dependencies, false positives, and expected alert semantics.
Use stable IDs and meaningful change history.
Retest after schema/parser changes and major backend upgrades.

quiz.question: What should normally change together with a detection rule?
options: Relevant regression tests and metadata such as dependencies or expected behavior
quiz.answer: Relevant regression tests and metadata such as dependencies or expected behavior
quiz.explanation: The test corpus and metadata provide the context needed to verify safe rule changes.

summary: Detection-as-code treats analytics as maintained software artifacts.
Tests and dependencies should be versioned with rule changes.
Change control reduces accidental coverage regressions.

tasks.title: Create a Detection Regression Pack
tasks.description: Build a small regression pack for one detection with positive, negative, boundary, and parser-change cases.
tasks.problemStatement: Create a set of JSONL fixtures and a reference evaluation procedure for the authentication detection from earlier modules. Include expected alert/no-alert outcomes and explain how you would run the tests after a parser or rule change.
objectives: Create at least four test cases.
requirements: Python 3.11+ or another environment that can parse JSONL.
tasks.hint: Treat test fixtures as executable specifications: each case should make the expected result unambiguous.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The regression pack should make it possible to tell whether a rule change altered intended behavior. In production, the test runner may be integrated with a detection-as-code pipeline; the essential requirement is that expected detections and non-detections remain explicit.

modules.title: Final Real-World Project: Local Incident Detection Pipeline
modules.description: Build and assess a complete local incident-detection reference pipeline that integrates telemetry validation, rule logic, correlation, scoring, evidence tracking, and regression testing.

lessons.title: Operational Detection Architecture
lessons.description: The final project begins by designing a small, vendor-neutral detection pipeline that ingests normalized JSONL events, evaluates deterministic rules, correlates related evidence, enriches findings, and emits analyst-readable incidents. The architecture intentionally uses Python standard-library components so students can run it locally without a cloud service or proprietary SIEM.
learningObjectives: Design a simple end-to-end incident detection architecture.
Define normalized event contracts and correlation keys.
Separate data ingestion, detection logic, enrichment, scoring, and reporting.
Explain the trust boundaries and limitations of a local reference implementation.

notes.text: Project architecture

JSONL events
    |
    v
Normalization/validation
    |
    +--> Rule: authentication burst
    +--> Rule: suspicious process context
    +--> Rule: unusual outbound connection
    |
    v
Correlation + enrichment
    |
    v
Risk scoring / incident grouping
    |
    v
JSON incident report + analyst evidence

The project is not a production SIEM. It is a transparent teaching reference for detection reasoning. Production systems add durable storage, streaming ingestion, identity/asset enrichment, access controls, distributed execution, monitoring, rule management, and formal incident workflows.
Use only synthetic or authorized telemetry in the project. The included event set is designed for local detection logic and does not execute or deliver malicious content.

quiz.question: Why does the project separate detection logic from reporting?
options: It makes rules easier to test, reuse, and maintain independently of presentation.
It removes the need for correlation.
quiz.answer: It makes rules easier to test, reuse, and maintain independently of presentation.
quiz.explanation: Layer separation improves testability and keeps detection semantics independent from output formatting.

summary: The final architecture is intentionally layered.
Normalized events allow rules to operate on stable concepts.
The reference implementation is a learning system, not a production SIEM.

lessons.title: Capstone Readiness and Deployment Boundaries
lessons.description: This lesson prepares students to implement and assess the final project. It covers input validation, safe test data, predictable outputs, limitations, and what must be added before a classroom detector could become a production service.
learningObjectives: Validate input data before detection.
Run deterministic tests against synthetic data.
Identify production gaps in a local detection reference implementation.
Define measurable acceptance criteria for the capstone.

items: Input contract: required fields and valid event types.
Determinism: the same test dataset should produce the same findings.
Traceability: each incident should list supporting event IDs.
Safety: project data and tests remain synthetic/authorized.
Acceptance: expected test scenarios produce the intended detections and benign scenarios remain quiet.

notes.text: Productionization would require secure deployment, authenticated data ingestion, access control, durable storage, alert routing, observability, key management, data retention policy, and integration with the organization’s incident-response process.
A local file-based detector must not be presented as equivalent to a managed enterprise SIEM or XDR platform.

quiz.question: What is the most important acceptance criterion for the final detector?
options: It produces expected findings on defined positive cases and avoids unintended findings on defined negative cases.
It uses the newest programming language.
quiz.answer: It produces expected findings on defined positive cases and avoids unintended findings on defined negative cases.
quiz.explanation: Detection correctness is evaluated by explicit, repeatable behavior—not by code size or novelty.

summary: Capstone success is defined by repeatable detection behavior.
Production boundaries and limitations should be explicit.
Synthetic/authorized data keeps the lab controlled.

project.name: Local Incident Detection Pipeline
project.description: A vendor-neutral reference detector that processes normalized JSONL telemetry, validates required fields, applies deterministic identity and endpoint rules, correlates process and network evidence, assigns explainable severity/confidence, and writes an analyst-readable incident report. All test data is synthetic and the implementation uses only the Python standard library.
steps: Create a local project directory and save the provided detector.py, tests.py, sample_events.jsonl, and README.md contents as the corresponding files.
Run the unit tests and fix any environment-specific path issues before analyzing output.
Run detector.py against sample_events.jsonl and inspect the incident report.
Trace each incident back to the supporting event IDs in the JSONL input.
Modify one threshold in a controlled branch, add a regression fixture for the intended behavior, and rerun the tests.
Add one new benign fixture that should not trigger the authentication rule and verify the regression suite remains green.
Document one production limitation and one telemetry gap that would change the confidence of the detector in an enterprise environment.
Treat the final output as an analytical reference, not as automatic proof of compromise or an automated containment system.

code.tests.py:
import json
import tempfile
import unittest
from pathlib import Path
from detector import load_events, build_incidents

class DetectionTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_sample_data_has_incidents(self):
        data = Path(__file__).with_name("sample_events.jsonl")
        events = load_events(data)
        incidents = build_incidents(events)
        rules = {item["incident_type"] for item in incidents}
        self.assertIn("authentication-burst-followed-by-success", rules)
        self.assertIn("suspicious-process-with-network-egress", rules)

    def test_benign_two_failures_do_not_trigger_auth_burst(self):
        lines = [
            {"event_id":"a1","timestamp":"2026-09-07T13:00:00Z","event_type":"authentication","outcome":"failure","user":"u1","source_ip":"192.0.2.8","target":"srv"},
            {"event_id":"a2","timestamp":"2026-09-07T13:01:00Z","event_type":"authentication","outcome":"failure","user":"u1","source_ip":"192.0.2.8","target":"srv"},
            {"event_id":"a3","timestamp":"2026-09-07T13:02:00Z","event_type":"authentication","outcome":"success","user":"u1","source_ip":"192.0.2.8","target":"srv"},
        ]
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
            p = Path(tmp) / "events.jsonl"
            p.write_text("\n".join(json.dumps(x) for x in lines), encoding="utf-8")
            events = load_events(p)
            incidents = build_incidents(events)
            self.assertFalse(any(i["incident_type"] == "authentication-burst-followed-by-success" for i in incidents))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()
code.README.md:
# Incident Detection Capstone

This reference implementation is a local, deterministic detector for synthetic normalized telemetry. It demonstrates ingestion, validation, rule evaluation, correlation, evidence collection, and incident reporting.

## Requirements
- Python 3.11 or newer is recommended.
- No third-party packages are required.

## Run

```bash
python detector.py sample_events.jsonl --output incidents.json
python -m unittest tests.py
```

The sample dataset includes an authentication burst followed by a successful login and an office-to-PowerShell process chain followed by a network event. These are synthetic teaching examples and do not execute any of the represented behaviors.

## Production boundary

The project is not a production SIEM/XDR platform. Production use would require authenticated ingestion, durable storage, access control, secret management, monitoring, retention policy, rule deployment controls, alert routing, and integration with the organization’s incident-response process.

project.explanation: The detector has five logical layers. First, load_events parses JSONL records, validates required fields by event type, and normalizes timestamps to UTC. Second, deterministic rules identify an authentication burst followed by a success and an office-launched script interpreter. Third, correlate_process_network links endpoint process evidence to matching network records on the same host and process context. Fourth, build_incidents turns findings into analyst-facing incident objects with severity and confidence labels and explicit supporting event IDs. Fifth, the tests encode expected positive and negative behavior. The design demonstrates the course principle that detection quality is a combination of data contracts, analytic logic, correlation, context, and regression testing. It intentionally avoids external packages so students can run it locally. A production implementation would need authenticated collection, resilient storage, access control, secrets handling, monitoring, rule lifecycle management, and integration with organizational incident response. The project does not execute any represented malicious behavior; all inputs are synthetic JSON records.
